foods.name: Brewed coffee
foods.tagline: The caffeine isn't the problem. The water gets there first.
overview: Brewed coffee is 99.39 g water per 100 g, with 40 mg of caffeine, 49 mg of potassium and 2 mg of sodium (USDA). A cup is 237 g, so about 95 mg of caffeine.

Caffeine, with a rat oral LD50 of 192 mg/kg, would take about 33.6 kg of coffee. Water sets the headline instead, at about 6.3 kg. Nobody is drinking six-odd kilos of coffee, and it's the water, not the coffee, doing the limiting.

foods.funFact: USDA lists brewed coffee at 40 mg of caffeine per 100 g, so a 237 g cup carries roughly 95 mg.

foods.name: Cola

foods.name: Orange juice

foods.name: Cassia cinnamon
foods.tagline: Coumarin is the story, and the real limit is far below the lab one.
overview: USDA's ground cinnamon is 10.58% water with 431 mg potassium and 10 mg sodium per 100 g, and doesn't say if it's cassia or Ceylon. BfR puts cassia at about 300 mg coumarin per 100 g on average. A teaspoon is 2.6 g.
Coumarin, with a rat oral LD50 of 293 mg/kg, sets the headline at about 6.8 kg, roughly 2,630 teaspoons. The lethal number is silly; the real limit, a tolerable daily intake, is much lower.

flagged.name: Honey
flagged.reason: borderline: the largest sugar (fructose) has no credible sourced rat LD50, so the headline cannot be trusted to stay above 2,000 g
flagged.details: USDA FDC 169640 (SR Legacy). Sugars (total, glucose LD50 as stand-in): 82,120 mg per 100 g, rat-derived 25,800.0 mg/kg, so 2,199 g; Glucose: 35,750 mg per 100 g, rat-derived 25,800.0 mg/kg, so 5,052 g; Water: 17,100 mg per 100 g, rat-derived 90,000.0 mg/kg, so 36,842 g; Potassium (as KCl): 52 mg per 100 g, rat-derived 1,363.6 mg/kg, so 183,562 g. A figure of 4,000 mg/kg appears only in small-distributor SDS copies (e.g. https://www.drm-chem.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/fructose-SDS.pdf), which looks implausibly low next to sucrose at 29,700 mg/kg; if it were used, honey would come to about 684 g (plausible). flagged.name: Black pepper
flagged.reason: plausible: piperine gives about 1,644 g (under 2,000 g), and real pepper often has more piperine than the minimum used here
flagged.details: Piperine 2.5% of dry weight is the USP monograph minimum (https://doi.usp.org/USPNF/USPNF_M7084_01_01.html); with USDA FDC 170931 moisture of 12.46 g per 100 g that is 2,188.5 mg per 100 g as sold. Piperine: 2,188.5 mg per 100 g, rat-derived 514.0 mg/kg, so 1,644 g; Potassium (as KCl): 1,329 mg per 100 g, rat-derived 1,363.6 mg/kg, so 7,182 g; Sodium (as NaCl): 20 mg per 100 g, rat-derived 1,180.2 mg/kg, so 413,070 g. Higher real piperine content would lower the lethal mass further.

problems: USDA FoodData Central API (DEMO_KEY) was rate-limited (HTTP 429) and the FDC food-page URLs are a JavaScript app that returned 404 to a plain fetch, so all composition figures come from the official SR Legacy bulk CSV. compositionSource.url is that dataset download (https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/fdc-datasets/FoodData_Central_sr_legacy_food_csv_2018-04.zip) and `id` is the FDC id inside it.

PubChem sources cite the PUG-View JSON URLs actually fetched (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/rest/pug_view/data/compound/<CID>/JSON), not the human-readable compound pages, which could not be fetched.

Fructose has no credible rat oral LD50 (PubChem: only a rabbit IV value; Fisher fructose SDSs: no LD50). A 4,000 mg/kg figure appears only in small-distributor SDS copies and looks wrong next to sucrose (29,700 mg/kg). So fructose is not used as a constituent, and wherever USDA gives only total sugars (cola, orange juice, milk chocolate, ketchup, jam) the total is treated as glucose (25,800 mg/kg, the lowest sourced sugar value) and labelled as a stand-in.

Water is the headline constituent for brewed coffee, black tea, green tea, cola, orange juice and hot sauce (about 6.3 to 7.2 kg). The only rat figure for water is a ">90 mL/kg" limit value from an SDS, not a true median, and I used 90,000 mg/kg to match the site's existing water entry. They clear the 5,000 g "absurd" cut-off by rule, but that is the same order of magnitude as litres of drink, and drinking too much water too fast is dangerous in its own right, so the realWorldCaveat on each says so plainly. Consider whether the site wants to show these at all.
Caffeine is not the limiting constituent in any drink (e.g. coffee about 33.6 kg vs water about 6.3 kg).
Jam: USDA has no strawberry jam entry, so the generic "Jams and preserves" (FDC 169641) was used and the food is named just "Jam" with strawberry jam as an alias.
Orange juice uses the USDA entry "chilled, includes from concentrate" (FDC 169100), a mix of juice types; the raw juice entry (FDC 169098) was not used.

Hot sauce uses the USDA TABASCO entry (FDC 174528). Capsaicin is not in USDA, its only PubChem oral LD50 values I saw are for mouse, and acetic acid in the sauce is not listed, so only water, sodium, potassium and vitamin C are modelled.

Cassia cinnamon: USDA does not say whether its ground cinnamon is cassia or Ceylon. Coumarin content (about 3,000 mg/kg average, up to 10,000 mg/kg maximum) is from the BfR FAQ, not a food composition table. The 3,000 mg/kg average is the working value (about 6,837 g); at the 10,000 mg/kg maximum it is about 2,051 g, still "large". Coumarin rat LD50 is 293 mg/kg (PubChem); mouse 196 and guinea pig 202 mg/kg also seen.

White vinegar: USDA does not list acetic acid, so the 5% strength comes from the Fisher SDS for vinegar (the same SDS gives the 3,310 mg/kg rat LD50). PubChem rat values are higher (3,530 and 4,665 mg/kg).
Olive oil: USDA reports undifferentiated 18:1 monounsaturated fat; in olive oil it is mostly oleic acid but bound in triglycerides, so the free oleic acid LD50 (74,000 mg/kg) is a stand-in.

Black pepper moved to flagged: piperine rat LD50 (514 mg/kg, adult female rats, PubMed 6857729) with the USP monograph minimum of 2.5% piperine on a dry basis gives about 1,644 g (plausible). Real pepper often contains more piperine, which would only lower this. I did not find a measured average piperine content in an openable source (ScienceDirect and ResearchGate are blocked), so the USP minimum was used.

Soy sauce and honey are also flagged. Soy sauce is plausible (sodium about 1,504 g). Honey is borderline because its biggest sugar, fructose, has no credible LD50; on the glucose stand-in it is about 2,199 g, and the unreliable 4,000 mg/kg fructose figure would drop it to about 684 g. Marmite (yeast extract spread, sodium about 2,444 g) is just inside "large" but is flagged conservatively as very salty; USDA's entry is generic yeast extract spread, not necessarily Marmite.
No oxalate data were found in USDA for these foods, so oxalate was not considered.
Sodium and potassium LD50s each rest on one primary source (NaCl from PubChem 3,000 mg/kg; KCl from a NIST SDS 2,600 mg/kg), so confidence for foods headlined by them is "medium" at best.
meta.count is 20, the number of foods researched; 16 are in `foods` and 4 are in `flagged`.
